title: Papildu dokumenti (Position paper of the Republic of Latvia on the Application of International Law in Cyberspace)
text: POSITION  PAPER OF THE REPUBLIC OF LATVIA  ON THE APPLICATION OF INTERNATIONAL LAW IN CYBERSPACE Introduction The modern digital, technologically advanced ,  and interconnected world is experiencing an increase in  the  s cale, scope, sophistication ,  and   complexity of malicious  activities in  cyber space.  Consequently ,  the   issue of  the   application of international law in cyberspace become s   increasingly   more important . The Republic of Latvia  reiterates its commitment to  a  rules-based international  order  and   asserts that international law, including  the  U nited  N ations  Charter in its entirety, is applicable in cyberspace.  As States have  already  recogni s ed ,  international law is “essential to maintaining peace and stability and promoting an open, secure, stable, accessible and peaceful information and communications technology environment”.   In the  current  geopolitical and  technolog ical  landscape , issues concerning  the protection of  information and communication technology (ICT)  and ensuring cybersecurity  are  becoming increasingly important .   ICTs  are becoming  progressively  more integral  in   the daily operations of societ ies , including for governments and non-State entities,  therefore  security risk s  for ICT users  are increasing .   Furthermore, the new information age requires innovative and rapid ly adaptive   tools  to  continuously  respon d  to the challenges presented by the malicious use of  ICTs .  From   a  legal perspective , both domestic  and international  law  can   be  applied  to  protect from and respond to such  malicious  cyber  activities . T he  mis use of  cyber  capabilities and other malicious activities  as  a  tool for disrupting critical  infrastructure ,   including  critical  ICT   infrastructure and  civilian infrastructure ,  has increased in recent years,  most notably in the context of the Russian Federation’s war of aggression against Ukraine . Due to the growing  number   of  malicious use of ICTs   against  States globally, the Republic of Latvia  views  the development of a national position on the application of international law in cyberspace  as  a positive step towards  strengthening   the  capacity and preparedness for  po tential   cyber threats , incidents, and  attack s  in a way that ensures compliance  with the  obligations  of States   under   the  international law . The Republic of Latvia  contends  that the utility in developing a national position on the application of international law in cyberspace is threefold. Firstly, it provides a reference  to   a  consolidat ed   understanding and opinion of the extent, complexity, and degree  of  applicability of international law in cyberspace  of  a given State .  As such,  a national position may also provide more clarity regarding the  opinio  juris  and potential State practice of the State concerned . Secondly, i t  adds to the efforts on   global development and interpretation of general rules of  the  application   of international law  in  cyberspace .  N ational positions  address   the  core aspects of  the norms of international law and   strengthen   States’  respect   for  a rules-based international order .   A  growing  number   of States and regional organisations have and continue to affirm  the  applicability  of international law  to cyberspace.  To this end, national positions are an effective tool  in   brid ging the gap in understanding  how international law applies in cyberspace . Thirdly, the development of national positions increases both state-level  and international  cooperation . Sharing each State’s  analysis  of the applicable law  can both  aid other States in formulating their own positions  and   ensur e  more clarity ,  predictability , and mutual understanding  of  both  the  global  legal  practices and  cyber  threats . On the whole,  position papers  provide  a  guiding material on  the principles and rules applicable  to hold States accountable in case of malicious activities in cyberspace . In creating  the present position paper , the Republic of Latvia contribute s  to the  development  of  a  more widespread understanding of  the applica tion   of  international law   in cyberspace  and promote s  responsible  State  behaviour  in cyberspace . Other areas of international law  PAGEREF _Toc220878846 \h  13 The  A pplication of  I nternational  L aw in  C yberspace The Republic of Latvia asserts that  the   existing international law applies  in i ts entirety   in   cyberspace.   The U nited  N ations (UN)  Charter,  international human rights law and international humanitarian law,  as well as customary international law,  are relevant  to State conduct  in cyber space .   State sovereignty As a cornerstone principle of international law, state s overeignty is  a binding rule of customary international law and applies  in  cyberspace.   I n  line  with their international legal obligations,  S tates exercise  sovereign authority  over  their   cyber infrastructure , persons  associated with the  S tate ,  and activities that occur within States’ sovereign territory.  This is also applicable in the context of a coastal State’s sovereignty over any submarine cables on the seabed beneath a State’s territorial sea , as well as airspace  above its territory .  Accordingly, States must not infringe upon another State’s sovereignty through the  cyber operations  they conduct. A violation of the principle of sovereignty will  also  be found if  a State interferes with  cyber  infrastructure  aboard a platform   that  enjoys sovereign immunity, no matter its location .   Even if the act does not  contravene  the principle of non-intervention or the prohibition of the use or threat of force, the violation of  the  obligation of States to respect another State’s sovereignty may nonetheless constitute an internationally wrongful act. The exercise of state sovereignty is subject to the right of self-defence  (see section 5 , subsection “The Right to Self-Defence” )  and any actions authorised by the UN Security Council (UNSC), as set out in Article 51 of the UN Charter. J urisdiction Domestic  jurisdiction A State may exercise jurisdiction over cyber activities and  ICTs  located on its territory ,  cyber  activities originating in or completed on its territory,   or   cyber  activities  hav ing  a substantial effect  i n its territory .   If  cyber   infrastructure   is physically or legally present within the State’s terri tory , jurisdiction  can  be  established .  States remain entitled to regulat e their  internal processes freely under national law, subject to  their  international legal obligations.  E xercis ing  State  jurisdiction  abroad A State may also  establish   jurisdiction extraterritorially in accordance with applicable international law .  Jurisdiction may be prescribed to cyber activities  extraterritorially  if  they  can be attributed to the State.   Non-Intervention The principle of  non-intervention , as  follows from  the principle of sovereign equality of States ,   foresees   the obligation of a State not  to  interfere in the domestic affairs of another State .  The prohibition  provides that a State is not to  intervene   in  the domestic or internal affairs of another State ( i.e.,  its  domaine   réservé ). Accordingly, the  issue  concerned is  the “choice of a political, economic, social, and cultural system, and the formulation of foreign policy” , as described by the  International Court of Justice ( ICJ )  in the  Nicaragua  v. United States   case .   If such sovereign choice is impacted through coercive means, the intervention can be considered as prohibited.   W hether  a  wrongful or  prohibited  intervention would constitute a use of force is  contingent   up on the  severity of the intervention . The Republic of Latvia considers  that  interference by a State may be found in instances of manipulating internal  processes  which   result in   significantly  undermining the ability to provide services within the injured State .   Targeted disinformation campaigns  enabled by the malicious use of ICTs  may constitute  a  prohibited   intervention if  they   use  “ methods of coercion in regard to such choices, which must remain free ones ” .   For example, a   State’s intentional interference  with  another State’s  electoral process  by  way of  malicious use of ICTs may also result in a violation of the principle of non-intervention.  Even if the cyber  operation does not constitute a violation  of  the principle of non-intervention, it may still amount to a violation of the principle of  S tate sovereignty. State Responsibility  and Attribution State responsibility is a core customary international law principle , and its key tenets are summarized in the International Law Commission’s  Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts ( ARSIW A) . A State is internationally responsible for every internationally wrongful act it commits.   Thus, l iability will be established if the internationally wrongful act is attributable to the State and breaches an international obligation of the State.  Consequently, a  S tate is responsible for the  actions conducted by its own organs acting with governmental authority.   Additionally, in cyber operations, a State which aids or assists another State in committing an internationally wrongful act  is responsible if it does so knowingly and the act would be an internationally wrongful act if committed by that State. Injured States must receive full reparation for the injury caused by the internationally wrongful act by way of restitution, compensation, and satisfaction.   Any injured State is entitled to invoke the responsibility of another State for breaching an obligation. If  an  internationally wrongful act  constitutes  a violation of an  erga   omnes  obligation  or an obligation that was owed to  all States or  a group of States, including the injured State , any State is entitled to invoke the responsibility of another State for the breach. To  invok e   S tate responsibility under international law , legal attribution must first be established . In the cyber context, attribution can be found where cyber operations are conducted by organs of a State or by persons or entities empowered by the law of the State to exercise elements of governmental authority.   A  cyber act conducted by a  non-State actor , whether a person or group of persons,  may  be attributed to the State i f the State exercises effective control  over the act ,   exercising elements of governmental authority in the absence or default of the official authorities ,  or accepts it as its own . The regime of State  responsibility  can only be invoked if legal attribution is established while political attribution may serve as  a  basis for political, diplomatic ,  or economic measures which do not require  circumstances  precluding wrongfulness for such measures to be lawful.  Consequently, t he Republic of Latvia views  that a  political decision to attribute a cyber operation to an actor is not equal to the rules of legal attribution outlined above. T he  P rohibition on the  Threat or  Use of Force As set out by Article 2(4) of the UN Charter,  the  threat or  use of force  is generally prohibited under international law.   Any such threat or use that is considered an act of aggression ,  as  defined in the UN General Assembly Resolution 3314 (1974) ,  shall also be prohibited.  A cyber  operation   amounts to  a  threat or  use of force when its scale and effects are comparable to  a kinetic   threat or  use of force.   However,  such cyber operations  may be permissible ,  subject to the rules  on   self-defence .  In addition, as stipulated in Article 39  of the UN Charter, the use of force may be authorised by the UNSC to maintain or restore international peace and security. The malicious use of ICTs may  nonetheless  constitute a prohibited intervention or a violation of the principle of  S tate sovereignty even if it does not reach the threshold of a threat or use of force. The Right of Self-Defence Flowing from the general prohibition on the  threat or  use of force ,  as set out in Article   51 of the UN Charter ,  a State’s  right  of  self-defence is an inherent individual or collective  right  in the event of an   imminent or  actual   armed attack.   The State’s  response  to an armed attack must be necessary and proportionate , whereafter any measures  taken  (including cyber-related) must immediately be reported to the U NSC .  The same rules may apply in instances where a State acts in self-defence to a cyber operation. For a cyber  operation  t o  warrant the right of self-defence , the  activities of the acting State  must reach a certain threshold  and be comparable in its scale and effects  to a kinetic attack .  As noted in the  Nicaragua  v. United States   case ,  the  operations   must be  “the  most grave  forms of the use of force”  to qualify as an armed attack .   In the same manner,  cyber operations  must also reach  this threshold  to  be deemed  an armed attack. Isolated  cases of  cyber  incidents   may not always amount to an armed attack. However,  related  incidents may be taken together and considered  cumulatively .   In such instances,  the Republic of Latvia contends that if the accumulation of  incidents  reaches a sufficient threshold of gravity, such cyber operations may amount to an armed attack.   Circumstances Precluding Wrongfulness Circumstances precluding wrongfulness, as set out  in  the  ARSIWA , describe six types of  conditions which render a  conduct  lawful  that would otherwise breach an international obligation of a State . The se   conditions  include:  consent , self-defence  (as set out above) , countermeasures ,  force majeure , distress ,  or  necessity . In invoking a circumstance precluding wrongfulness, a State provides a justification  for an act that would otherwise be considered a breach  of an international obligation.  Consent If valid consent has been given by the injured  S tate to the  S tate  responsible  for the commission of an internationally wrongful act, the  S tate  responsible  shall not be accountable to the extent of the consent given. Countermeasures As set out in Article 22  of ARSIWA , a n injured  State may resort to countermeasures against the State  responsible  for an internationally wrongful act . Such measures  may  also   be  conducted  by cyber means .   The purpose of such  counter measures is to ensure that the  S tate responsible for committing the internationally wrongful act resumes its compliance with its obligations under international law.   Moreover, countermeasures sha ll only be taken as an interim measure, for the duration of time the responsible State is not performing its international obligations.  As s uch  actions  would be considered unlawful but for the internationally wrongful act committed by the offending  S tate, the actions engaged by the injured  S tate must be      proportionate .   The proportionality of a countermeasure is assessed based on whether the act was  “ commensurate with the injury suffere d, taking into account the gravity of the internationally wrongful act and the rights in question”.   In addition, there may be instances where the countermeasures taken by an injured State are not sufficient in successfully responding to  the   State committing an internationally wrongful act , if such an  act breaches an  erga   omnes  obligation . In such instances,  other  States  may  support  the injured State’s countermeasure efforts by  engaging in collective countermeasures . Force majeure Should an irresistible force or an unforeseen event, beyond the control of the State,  occur,  making it materially impossible to perform an obligation owed by the responsible State to the injured State, the  responsible  State shall be precluded from wrongfulness.  The aforementioned   will  not apply if the responsible State has caused the  force majeure  or if the injured State has assumed the risk of the situation to occur. Distress Should an act not in conformity with an international obligation be committed in distress, with no other reasonable way to act in the given situation, the wrongfulness of said act shall be precluded.  The aforementioned  will not apply if the act in question is likely to create a comparable or greater peril   than compliance with the obligation in question . Necessity Necessity may preclude an act not in conformity with an international obligation from being wrongful if it is  the only way for the State to safeguard an essential interest against a grave and imminent peril and does not seriously impair the interest of the State towards which the obligation is owed, or the entire international community.  The  aforementioned will  not apply i f  the obligation excludes the possibility of invoking necessity or  if  the  responsible  State contributed to the situation of necessity.   Due  D iligence Acknowledging   the  States’ right to control activities within its territory, States  must  exercise due  diligence  not to knowingly permit its territory to be used for unauthorised and harmful actions against other States.   To this end, a   S tate must take  all  appropriate  and   reasonably available   measures  if it has or should have knowledge of a cyber activity, the origin of which derives from the cyber infrastructure on its territory,  or  territory over  which it  exercises effective  control,  that violates the rights of another State.   There is no need for physical  impact or harm  to be present,  and serious adverse impact  on   significant and legally protected interests of another State   suffices ,  to engage the due diligence principle.   Furthermore, due diligence may also be relevant in situations where  cyber  operations  are conducted  by  one private entity located in one State to another private entity in another State.  The application of the principle in such cases would apply if the State in which the attacking private entity is based in knew or ought to have known about the  cyber  operations  committed  and failed to take reasonable measures to cease activities  causing   serious  adverse consequences . The standard  or threshold  for  harm is assessed in an objective manner ,  taking into account  the obligation s  of the State under  i nternational  l aw  and the circumstances of the case.  P ossible  future technological  and scientific  advancements  may also be considered in such assessments .   Peaceful Settlement of Disputes Notwithstanding the right of self-defence, countermeasures, and other lawful actions under international  law,  international  disputes shall be settled peacefully .  The means of peaceful settlement of disputes includes , but is not limited to,   diplomatic measures,  negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, and judicial settlement. Regional agencies or arrangements, or other peaceful means may be engaged to resolve disputes.  Additionally ,  States can turn to the  UNSC   to settle disputes among themselves . Retorsions In addition to circumstances precluding wrongfulness and the peaceful settlement of disputes, States  may also respond to  internationally   wrongful conduct , including  the use or threat of force by way of  either individual or collective  retorsions .  Such acts are  “unfriendly” but lawful, and may include  a prohibition of or limitation of diplomatic relations or lawful economic or financial restrictive measures .     International  H uman  R ights  L aw The Republic of Latvia reaffirms that international human rights law applies both online and offline. Accordingly, international human rights obligations established by applicable international treaties, as well as customary international law are fully applicable in cyberspace.  The Republic of Latvia maintains that the rights and freedoms, including but not limited to the freedom of expression and opinion, including the right to seek, receive, and impart information, and the right to respect for one’s private life, are directly connected to cyberspace and thus shall apply in this context.  Any restrictions on human rights in the cyber context, including but not limited to restrictions on targeted disinformation campaigns enabled by the malicious use of ICTs, must be justified and require certain conditions to be met, such that they must be established by law,  pursue a legitimate aim, and  be necessary and proportionate.  Furthermore, the Republic of Latvia underlines that malicious use of ICTs and the consequences of cyber activities  that threaten the life of the nation   can constitute grounds for a State to exercise its rights to derogate from its human rights treaty obligations when permitted and under the conditions established by the treaty in question.   International  H umanitarian  L aw T he Republic of Latvia  contends  that international humanitarian law  (IHL)  applies in cyberspace.  In accordance with Common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions, States are under an obligation to respect and ensure respect for the rules and principles of international humanitarian law outlined in the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols  in all circumstances .  Moreover, the Republic of Latvia assert s  that  the application of IHL  does not lead to the militarisation of cyberspace  and that the acceptance of it in the cyber context does not promote cyber warfare .  Rather, it supports the use of different international legal regimes in various legal contexts.  IHL  can apply in cyberspace where  cyber   operations  are carried out in relation to armed conflicts that may be international or non-international in nature , subject to the different requirements for qualifying each type of armed conflict .  The rul es of  IHL , which include  the principle of humanity, military necessity, distinction, proportionality, and the obligation to take all feasible precautions , apply in cyberspace .  Particular attention must be paid to the principle of distinction  both in terms of civilians and combatants and civil ian objects  and military objectives, especially  where  ICTs   are  concerned.  In addition,  cyber   infrastructure   which  is  not  a  military objective  is  protected as  a  civilian object .   As a general rule of IHL, civilians and civilian objects must be protected .   Civilians enjoy protection, unless and for such time as they are directly participating in hostilities.  Additionally, indiscriminate attacks are prohibited. Cyber operations may be considered an attack under  IHL , that is, as an act of violence againt the adversary, whether in offence of in defence.   Neutrality  As a key tenet of international law, t he law of neutrality applies in cyberspace. Therefore, States are prohibited from attacking neutral cyber infrastructure.  Furthermore, belligerents are prohibited from the use of neutral cyber infrastructure in neutral territory   for the exercise of belligerent rights .  A   neutral State  shall  not knowingly allow parties to the conflict  to  exercise belligerent rights from cyber infrastructure located in its territory or under its control.     International Criminal Law   The Republic of Latvia affirms that international criminal law is applicable in cyberspace. Cyber operations may amount to international crimes such as genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, or the crime of aggression, and therefore give rise to individual criminal responsibility.  This can include individual commission, joint commission, and commission through others, as well as attempted commission of all three aforementioned forms of perpetration.   Commanders and other superiors can be found criminally responsible if they knew or should have known about the commission, or plan to commit, international crimes through cyber activities, and failed to take reasonable measures to prevent such acts from occurring in cyberspace, provided that said activities amount to an international crime.     Consequently, the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC) applies to cyberspace.  As a court of last resort, if all other options have been  exhausted  at the national level, the ICC can decide cases against individuals who have been alleged to have committed international crimes in cyberspace.   Diplomatic and Consular Law   The Republic of Latvia contends that the rules and principles of diplomatic and consular law, as reflected in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations  (VCDR) and the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations  (VCCR), apply in cybe rspace .  As a general rule, diplomatic and consular premises are inviolable and may only be entered by authorities and agents of the receiving State with the consent of the head of the consular post or his designee or the head of the diplomatic mission of the sending State .   This includes any property located within the premises, including cyber infrastructure. The receiving State shall ensure the protection of the premises of a sending State’s diplomatic mission or consular post against any intrusion or damage and to prevent any disturbance of their peace and impairment of dignity .  The inviolability of  official  correspondence  and communications  also extends to data in transit and to data accessed remotely.  Thus, the interception of such correspondence or communications is prohibited and applies to all States. In addition, the mission and consular post of the sending State shall enjoy free communication for all official purposes .  The official correspondence  and the archives  of the  diplomatic mission or the  consular post shall also be inviolable , which  may also apply to digitally stored correspondence and archives .   In any case, persons enjoying privileges and immunities under the VCDR and  the  VCCR shall respect the laws and regulations of the receiving State and shall not interfere in its internal affairs.   Moreover, the premises of the diplomatic mission and consular posts may not be  purposely  used in a way that is inconsistent with the rule s  laid down in the VCDR and the VCCR, respectively ,  including by way of  malicious   cyber activities .   O ther  areas of international law Although not exhaustive, t he Republic of Latvia considers the following  aspects of different  areas of international law , which  have  not  been  mentioned   previously  in this position paper,   to be of particular importance  in the context of cyberspace . Law of the Sea The rules regarding state sovereignty and  the exercise of  jurisdiction apply to vessels  and  artificial islands and installations used to engage in cyber operations  (as discussed in sections 1 and 2) .   In the context of international maritime law,  the flag State of the vessel conducting cyber operations  shall exercise  exclusive jurisdiction over  the m  in  accordance with Article s  91 and 92 of  the  UN  Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) .   In addition,  the international law  applicable to submarine cables  shall also apply  in relation to submarine communication cables , in particular the   rules regarding the breaking or injury of a submarine cable .   For example, a  submarine communication cable may  be injured by use of physical tapping , leading to the interference with  network traffic . Air law States may conduct cyber operations in international airspace , subject to restrictions thereon under international law .  However, they  must be conducted having due regard for the safety of international civil aviation. Space  Law Any cyber operations conducted in outer  space, including  on  the Moon and other celestial bodies, must be carried out in accordance with international law and the UN Charter.   States retain jurisdiction and control over any space objects appearing on their national registry. Additionally, States must  conduct their activities in   outer space with due regard for the corresponding interests of other States so as not to interfere with their peaceful space activities . States must ensure that  national  – both governmental and non-governmental –  cyber activities in outer space  are conducted in conformity with international space law.
